title: 700,000-Year-Old Squirrel Poop Reveals a Lost Ecosystem—and a Mystery Species
summary:
Frozen, ice-age squirrel poop doesn't stink—at first. But thaw it out, and the smell hits you like a wall. "There's no mistaking. This is a very poopy-smelling lab," says archaeologist Tyler Murchie, who studies ancient DNA at the Hakai Institute in Canada.

That smelly poop turned out to be a scientific goldmine. Miners digging for gold in the Yukon melted permafrost—permanently frozen ground—and exposed ancient squirrel burrows. Inside, they found tunnels, food caches, and little latrines (bathrooms) frozen in time. Murchie's team thawed 13 fecal pellets and extracted DNA—the molecule that carries an organism's genetic instructions.

The oldest pellet was nearly 700,000 years old. Others dated to between 80,000 and 17,000 years ago, during the Pleistocene epoch—a period of alternating ice ages and warm spells. The DNA revealed what the squirrels ate: grasses, willows, beetles, grasshoppers—and surprisingly, bits of woolly mammoth, steppe bison, wolves, and ancient horses.

Don't picture squirrels hunting mammoths. Paleontologist Jacquelyn Gill, who wasn't part of the study, explains they were likely scavenging—chewing on bones for calcium, as rodents do today. Murchie recalls watching a squirrel on his fence eating a bone.

But the biggest surprise was the squirrels themselves. Scientists assumed Pleistocene squirrels were the same species as modern Yukon squirrels. "The species we thought these all were doesn't seem to actually be the species that's there today," Murchie says. The oldest sample sits on its own evolutionary branch—possibly a new species, with its closest living relatives in China.

This research, published June 9 in Nature Communications, shows how a humble pile of ancient poop can paint a vivid picture of an entire ecosystem—and rewrite what we thought we knew.
why_it_matters: Ancient poop might sound gross, but this study shows how small biological clues can reveal entire ecosystems and even change what we know about species. Understanding how Ice Age animals and plants responded to climate shifts can help scientists think about how today's Arctic ecosystems may respond to warming.

background_read: The Yukon (a far-north territory in Canada) is one of the best places on Earth to find Ice Age remains because its permafrost—ground that stays frozen for very long periods—can preserve organic material for hundreds of thousands of years.
During the Pleistocene epoch, a geological period of repeated ice ages that ended roughly 12,000 years ago, woolly mammoths, steppe bison, and ancient horses roamed this cold landscape.
Miners searching for gold in the Yukon have long disturbed the frozen ground, and their digging can accidentally expose ancient burrows, bones, and other preserved clues.
Ancient DNA research lets scientists identify the species in tiny samples, such as seeds, soil, or animal droppings, and sometimes reveals that a familiar species has deep, unexpected relationships.
The Hakai Institute, a Canadian research organization that supports coastal and environmental science, is one of the groups using these techniques to piece together past ecosystems.

perspectives.description: For scientists, this study is a win: DNA extracted from a few tiny poop pellets revealed a full Ice Age menu and a possible new species. It shows that overlooked, humble samples can drive major discoveries.

Permafrost is thawing because of climate change, and mining activities that expose ancient burrows can also damage them. Without careful study and preservation, these once-frozen time capsules could decay before they are fully understood.

The finding fits the larger pattern of ancient DNA studies overturning assumptions about how stable species are across time. It raises questions, rather than closing them, about where these squirrels came from and when the modern population appeared.

Future research could compare more Yukon squirrel DNA with the Chinese relatives to date exactly when the two branches split. It could also show how ecosystems responded to past warming, offering clues for a warming Arctic today.
